about: CIVE40005 Mechanics is a 5 ECTS core module in Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Civil Engineering, running across the autumn and spring terms (2026-27 programme specification). No public syllabus or module descriptor was available, so the topics in this pack are a standard first-year engineering mechanics course built from the module's title and short description (foundation engineering mechanics): vectors, forces and moments; equilibrium; distributed loads and centroids; friction; and the kinematics and kinetics of particles and rotating rigid bodies. Year 1 also has a separate core module, CIVE40006 Structural Mechanics 1, so some of the statics here (equilibrium, supports, distributed loads, centroids) may overlap with it or be taught there instead. Check the topic order and coverage against your own lecture materials. Assessment details could not be confirmed, so none are given.
topics: Equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies

notes.body:
Engineering mechanics is written in the language of vectors. Before tackling structures or moving bodies you need to handle forces and moments confidently in two and three dimensions.

Scalars and vectors
- A scalar has magnitude only (mass, time, energy). A vector has magnitude and direction (force, displacement, velocity).
- In Cartesian form F = F_x i + F_y j + F_z k, with magnitude |F| = √(F_x² + F_y² + F_z²).
- A unit vector in the direction of F is F/|F|. Direction cosines are its components: cos θ_x = F_x/|F|, and so on.
- To write a force along a line from point A to point B: find the position vector r_AB = r_B − r_A, divide by its length to get a unit vector, then multiply by the force magnitude. This is the standard way to handle cable forces in 3D.

Adding forces
- Add components, not magnitudes. Two perpendicular forces of 30 kN and 40 kN have a resultant of 50 kN at 53.1° to the 30 kN force.
- The parallelogram and triangle rules give the same answer graphically; the sine and cosine rules solve the triangle by hand.

Dot product
- A·B = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z = |A||B| cos θ.
- Uses: the angle between two lines, and the component of a force along a line (F·u, where u is a unit vector along the line).

Cross product
- A × B has magnitude |A||B| sin θ and is perpendicular to both, with direction from the right-hand rule.
- A × B = (A_yB_z − A_zB_y) i + (A_zB_x − A_xB_z) j + (A_xB_y − A_yB_x) k. Note that B × A = −A × B.

Moment of a force
- About a point O: M_O = r × F, where r runs from O to any point on the force's line of action.
- In 2D this reduces to M = F × perpendicular distance, or M_z = xF_y − yF_x (anticlockwise positive). For F = (3, 4) kN acting at (2, 1) m, M_z = 2 × 4 − 1 × 3 = 5 kN m anticlockwise.
- Varignon's theorem: the moment of a force equals the sum of the moments of its components. Splitting a force into components is often easiest.
- Moment about an axis through O with unit vector u: M_u = u·(r × F).

Couples
- Two equal and opposite parallel forces form a couple, M = Fd. A couple has no resultant force and the same moment about every point.
- A force can be moved to a new point if you add a couple equal to its moment about that point.

Units and checks
- Forces in N or kN, moments in N m or kN m. Keep units consistent and check that the answer's size is sensible.

Exam tips: in 3D problems, write position vectors and unit vectors explicitly; in 2D problems, sketch the perpendicular distance for every moment, or use components.

notes.h: Equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies
notes.body:
Most civil engineering structures are designed to stay still, so equilibrium is the first tool you use on beams, frames, cables and retaining walls.

Equilibrium conditions
- Particle: ΣF = 0, i.e. ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 (plus ΣF_z = 0 in 3D). A particle can only be in equilibrium under concurrent forces.
- Rigid body in 2D: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point: three independent equations, so at most three unknowns per body.
- Rigid body in 3D: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0, six scalar equations.

The free body diagram (FBD)
- Isolate the body, then draw every external force: self-weight at the centre of gravity, applied loads, and support reactions.
- Internal forces between parts of the same body do not appear.
- Choose reaction directions; a negative answer just means the arrow should point the other way.

Supports and their reactions (2D)
- Roller or smooth surface: one force, perpendicular to the surface.
- Pin (hinge): two force components.
- Fixed (built-in, encastré) support: two force components and a moment.
- Cable or rope: tension along the cable, pulling away from the body; it cannot push.
- Link (two-force member): force along the member, tension or compression.

Determinacy and stability
- A planar body with exactly three suitably arranged reaction components is statically determinate, so equilibrium alone gives the reactions.
- More than three gives a statically indeterminate (redundant) structure: you need compatibility and material behaviour (later modules).
- Fewer than three, or three reactions that are all parallel or all meet at one point, gives a mechanism (unstable).

Solving efficiently
- Take moments about a point where two unknowns act, to get the third directly.
- Use the remaining equations for the others, then check with an equation you did not use.
- Two-force members carry forces along the line joining their ends; three non-parallel forces in equilibrium must meet at a point.

Worked example: simply supported beam
Span 6 m, supports A (pin) and B (roller). A UDL of 4 kN/m acts over the full span, and a 12 kN point load acts 2 m from A.
- The UDL's resultant is 24 kN at 3 m.
- Moments about A: 6R_B = 12 × 2 + 24 × 3 = 96, so R_B = 16 kN.
- Vertical: R_A = 36 − 16 = 20 kN.
- Check, moments about B: 6R_A = 12 × 4 + 24 × 3 = 120, so R_A = 20 kN. Correct.

Particle example
A 500 N lamp hangs from two cables at 40° and 60° to the horizontal. Resolving horizontally and vertically gives T(40°) ≈ 254 N and T(60°) ≈ 389 N; the steeper cable carries more load.

Exam tips: draw a clear FBD with all reactions labelled before any algebra, say which point you take moments about, and always finish with a check equation.

notes.h: Distributed loads, centroids and centre of mass
notes.body:
Real loads are spread out: the self-weight of a slab, wind on a facade, soil pressure on a retaining wall. To use the equilibrium equations, each distributed load is replaced by an equivalent resultant acting at the right place.

Distributed loads on beams
- A line load w(x) is given in force per length (kN/m).
- Resultant = ∫w dx = the area of the load diagram.
- It acts through the centroid of the load diagram: x̄ = ∫x w dx/∫w dx.
- Uniform load w over length L: resultant wL at L/2.
- Triangular load from 0 to w₀ over L: resultant w₀L/2 at 2L/3 from the zero end (L/3 from the peak).
- Trapezoidal load: split into a rectangle and a triangle and treat each separately.
- Example: a load rising from 0 to 9 kN/m over 6 m has resultant 27 kN acting 4 m from the zero end.
- The equivalent resultant is valid for finding reactions, but not for internal forces within the loaded length.

Centre of gravity and centre of mass
- Centre of gravity: the point through which the total weight acts. For a body in a uniform gravity field it coincides with the centre of mass.
- x̄ = Σm_i x_i/Σm_i (discrete), or x̄ = ∫x dm/∫dm (continuous).
- For a homogeneous body of uniform thickness, the centre of mass is at the centroid of the shape.

Centroids of areas
- x̄ = ∫x dA/A and ȳ = ∫y dA/A. The integral ∫y dA is the first moment of area.
- Standard results: rectangle at its centre; triangle at one third of the height from the base; semicircle of radius r at 4r/(3π) from the diameter.
- Any axis of symmetry contains the centroid.

Composite shapes
- Split into simple parts, then x̄ = ΣA_i x̄_i/ΣA_i (likewise for ȳ).
- Holes are included as negative areas.
- A table (part, area, centroid, area × centroid) keeps the working tidy and earns method marks.

Worked example: T-section
A flange of 120 mm × 20 mm sits on top of a web of 20 mm × 100 mm (total height 120 mm). Measure y from the bottom of the web.
- Web: area 2000 mm², centroid at 50 mm.
- Flange: area 2400 mm², centroid at 110 mm.
- ȳ = (2000 × 50 + 2400 × 110)/4400 = 364 000/4400 ≈ 82.7 mm from the bottom (37.3 mm below the top).
- The centroid is pulled towards the larger area, the flange.

Why it matters for civil engineers
- Centroids locate the neutral axis of beams (needed in Structural Mechanics), resultants of soil and water pressure on walls, and the centre of gravity of structures for overturning checks.
- Overturning check: a wall is safe against toppling about its toe if the restoring moment of its weight exceeds the overturning moment of the lateral loads.

Exam tips: always state your datum, use a table for composite sections, and sanity-check that the centroid lies within the shape's extent and nearer to the heavier part.

Friction holds a ladder against a wall, stops a retaining wall sliding, and lets vehicles brake. It is also why loads on slopes and wedges need careful analysis.

Coulomb's laws of dry friction
- The friction force F acts tangentially to the contact surface and opposes the relative sliding (or the tendency to slide).
- No sliding: F takes whatever value equilibrium needs, up to F_max = μ_s N.
- Impending sliding: F = μ_s N exactly.
- Sliding: F = μ_k N, where μ_k is usually somewhat smaller than μ_s.
- To a good approximation F does not depend on the apparent area of contact.

The three cases in problems
- Equilibrium is unknown: assume no slip, solve for F and N, and check F ≤ μ_s N. If the check fails, the body slides, so recompute with F = μ_k N.
- Impending motion is stated ("on the point of slipping"): set F = μ_s N, with F opposing the impending motion.
- Motion is known: use F = μ_k N opposing the relative velocity.
- Example: a 200 kg crate (N = 1962 N) with μ_s = 0.4 is pushed with 700 N. F_max = 785 N > 700 N, so it stays put and friction is 700 N, not 785 N.

Angle of friction
- tan φ = μ_s. The resultant of N and F lies within an angle φ of the normal.
- A block on a slope is on the point of slipping under its own weight when the slope angle equals φ. Granular soils show the same idea: the angle of repose is related to the friction angle.

Inclined planes
- Resolve along and perpendicular to the slope: N = mg cos θ (if no other perpendicular forces).
- Force parallel to the slope to push a block up at impending motion: P = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ).
- Smallest such force to stop it sliding down (if tan θ > μ): P = mg(sin θ − μ cos θ).

Sliding or tipping
- A tall block pushed sideways may tip about its front edge before it slides.
- Sliding needs P = μW. Tipping needs P × h = W × (b/2), where h is the push height and b the base width.
- Whichever needs the smaller P happens first. Pushing higher makes tipping more likely.
- Civil example: retaining walls and gravity dams are checked against both sliding (friction at the base) and overturning (moments about the toe).

Wedges
- Used to lift or position heavy loads. Draw separate FBDs of each block with friction on every surface where sliding is impending, all opposing the motion.

Belts and ropes
- A rope wrapped round a post or bollard: T₁/T₂ = e^(μβ), with β in radians. A few turns let a small pull hold a very large load.

Exam tips: state clearly whether slip is impending, show friction opposing the (impending) motion, and never automatically write F = μN without justification.

Kinematics describes how things move (position, velocity and acceleration) without asking why. It underpins vehicle dynamics, falling objects on site and, later, structural vibration.

Rectilinear motion
- Velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt² = v dv/ds.
- Constant acceleration only: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t.
- If a depends on time, position or velocity, integrate instead (a = v dv/ds is useful when a depends on s).
- Graphs: the gradient of s–t is v and the gradient of v–t is a; the area under v–t is the displacement.
- Multi-stage motion (accelerate, cruise, brake): treat each stage separately, with the final values of one stage as the initial values of the next.
- Example: a car accelerates from rest at 2 m/s² for 10 s (100 m, reaching 20 m/s), then cruises for 5 s (100 m): 200 m in total.

Projectile motion (neglecting air resistance)
- Horizontal: constant velocity. Vertical: constant acceleration g downwards. Both share the same time.
- Thrown horizontally at u from height h: fall time t = √(2h/g); horizontal distance ut.
- Example: 15 m/s horizontally from a 20 m cliff gives t = 2.02 s and a distance of 30.3 m.
- On level ground with launch speed v at angle θ: range v² sin 2θ/g, maximum height (v sin θ)²/(2g).

Curvilinear motion: normal and tangential components
- The velocity is tangent to the path.
- a_t = dv/dt (changing speed); a_n = v²/ρ (changing direction), towards the centre of curvature.
- |a| = √(a_t² + a_n²).
- Example: a car on a bend of radius 100 m speeding up uniformly from 15 to 25 m/s in 8 s has a_t = 1.25 m/s². At 20 m/s, a_n = 4.0 m/s², so |a| ≈ 4.19 m/s².
- Highway and railway design limits a_n (passenger comfort and skidding), which is why bends have minimum radii and transition curves.

Cartesian and polar components
- Cartesian: a = ẍ i + ÿ j; useful for projectiles.
- Polar: v_r = ṙ, v_θ = rθ̇; a_r = r̈ − rθ̇², a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇. Useful when motion is described from a fixed point (for example a radar tracking a vehicle).

Relative motion
- r_B = r_A + r_B/A, so v_B/A = v_B − v_A. Use it for vehicles passing each other, or rain falling on a moving vehicle.

Exam tips: always check that acceleration is constant before using the suvat equations, draw a v–t sketch for multi-stage problems, and resolve projectile motion into independent horizontal and vertical parts.

notes.h: Kinetics of particles: Newton's second law
notes.body:
Kinetics relates forces to the motion they cause. The direct route is Newton's second law, applied with a free body diagram.

Newton's laws
- First: a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force.
- Second: ΣF = ma, valid in an inertial (non-accelerating) frame. Mass is the measure of inertia.
- Third: forces between two bodies are equal and opposite.
- Weight W = mg with g = 9.81 m/s². Mass is in kg and weight in N; mixing them up is a common error.

Method
- Draw the FBD with every real force (weight, normal reactions, friction, tensions, applied forces).
- Draw a kinetic diagram showing ma in a direction you choose as positive.
- Write ΣF = ma in suitable components (x–y, or n–t for curved paths).
- Add kinematic constraints (for example, connected bodies share an acceleration if the string is taut and inextensible).
- Solve, then check signs and units.

Common situations
- Lift (elevator): the floor reaction on a person of mass m accelerating upwards at a is N = m(g + a). An 80 kg person in a lift accelerating up at 2 m/s² feels about 945 N instead of 785 N.
- Connected bodies: for a 10 kg block on a smooth table pulled by a 5 kg hanging mass, a = 5g/15 ≈ 3.27 m/s² and the tension is 10a ≈ 32.7 N, less than the hanging weight.
- Friction during motion: use F = μ_k N, opposing the velocity.
- Braking on a level road: the maximum deceleration without skidding is μg. A car at 25 m/s with μ = 0.7 stops in about 45.5 m (ignoring reaction time).

Curved paths (n–t components)
- ΣF_n = mv²/ρ, towards the centre; ΣF_t = m dv/dt.
- The force towards the centre (friction on a flat bend, a component of the normal reaction on a banked bend, tension in a string) must be supplied by real forces. "Centrifugal force" does not appear on an FBD in an inertial frame.
- Flat bend: maximum speed √(μgr).
- Banked bend at angle θ without friction: design speed v = √(rg tan θ). Road and rail designers use banking (superelevation) so that vehicles at the design speed need little side friction.

Variable mass and other extensions
- If the force depends on velocity (for example air drag ∝ v²), write m dv/dt = F(v) and separate variables; a terminal velocity occurs where the net force is zero.

Exam tips: never write "ma" as a force on the FBD, keep the positive direction consistent across all bodies in a system, and check limiting cases (μ = 0, a = 0) to see that your expression behaves sensibly.

Integrating Newton's second law gives two powerful principles. Work and energy (integrating over distance) gives speeds without needing accelerations. Impulse and momentum (integrating over time) handles impacts and short, sharp forces such as pile driving.

Work
- Work done by a force: U = ∫F·ds. Only the force component along the displacement does work.
- Constant force: U = F s cos θ.
- Gravity: U = −mgΔh (negative when the body rises).
- Linear spring of stiffness k stretched from x₁ to x₂: U = −½k(x₂² − x₁²).
- Normal reactions on fixed surfaces do no work; friction does negative work μ_k N × distance.

Kinetic energy and the work–energy principle
- T = ½mv². Principle: T₁ + ΣU₁→₂ = T₂.
- If only conservative forces (gravity, springs) do work, total mechanical energy is conserved: T₁ + V₁ = T₂ + V₂, with V_g = mgh and V_e = ½kx².
- Example: a spring (k = 2000 N/m) compressed 0.1 m launches a 0.5 kg mass on a smooth surface: ½kx² = ½mv², so v = √(kx²/m) ≈ 6.32 m/s.

Power and efficiency
- P = dU/dt = F·v.
- A 1500 kg vehicle climbing a slope with sin θ = 0.05 at a steady 20 m/s needs P = mgv sin θ ≈ 14.7 kW just to overcome gravity.
- Efficiency η = output power/input power.

Impulse and momentum
- Linear momentum p = mv (a vector). Impulse ∫F dt = Δp.
- Useful when forces act over known times or are very large and brief (impacts), where the impulse is known but the force history is not.
- If the external impulse on a system is zero (or negligible during a short impact), total momentum is conserved.

Impacts
- Coefficient of restitution e = speed of separation/speed of approach (along the line of impact).
- e = 1: elastic (no kinetic energy lost). e = 0: perfectly plastic (bodies move together, maximum energy loss).
- Momentum is conserved in an impact even though kinetic energy is not.

Civil example: pile driving
- A hammer of mass M falls height h onto a pile of mass m.
- Speed before impact v = √(2gh) (energy conservation).
- Plastic impact: common speed V = Mv/(M + m) (momentum conservation). Some energy is lost in the blow.
- The pile and hammer then penetrate a distance s against the ground resistance R: (R − (M + m)g)s = ½(M + m)V² (work–energy).
- A heavier hammer relative to the pile wastes less energy in the impact.

Exam tips: choose energy for position-dependent problems, momentum for impacts and time-dependent forces, and never use energy conservation across an inelastic impact.

Many engineering objects rotate: winch drums on cranes, pulleys, turbines, gates on hinges. For these, size and shape matter, and we need angular versions of the particle equations.

Rotational kinematics
- Angular displacement θ (rad), angular velocity ω = dθ/dt (rad/s), angular acceleration α = dω/dt (rad/s²).
- Constant α: ω = ω₀ + αt; θ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ.
- A point at radius r: v = ωr; a_t = αr; a_n = ω²r towards the axis.
- 1 rev = 2π rad; rpm × 2π/60 = rad/s.
- A rope wound on a drum of radius r without slipping: the rope's speed and acceleration are ωr and αr.

Moment of inertia
- I = Σmr² = ∫r² dm: the rotational equivalent of mass. It depends on how mass is distributed about the axis.
- Standard results: thin rod about its centre mL²/12, about one end mL²/3; solid disc or cylinder about its axis mr²/2; thin ring mr².
- Parallel axis theorem: I = I_G + md², where d is the distance from the centroidal axis to the parallel axis. (For example, rod about its end: mL²/12 + m(L/2)² = mL²/3.)
- Radius of gyration k: I = mk².
- (The second moment of area used for beam bending in Structural Mechanics is the analogous quantity for areas.)

Equation of motion for rotation about a fixed axis
- ΣM_O = I_O α (moments about the fixed axis O).
- Plus force equations for the centre of mass G: ΣF = m a_G, used to find the reactions at the bearing or pivot.
- Example: a uniform rod of length L pivoted at one end and released from horizontal has initial angular acceleration α = (mgL/2)/(mL²/3) = 3g/(2L). For L = 2 m that is about 7.36 rad/s².

Connected systems: drum and hanging mass
- A mass m hangs from a rope wound on a drum (moment of inertia I, radius r).
- Mass: mg − T = ma. Drum: Tr = Iα. Constraint: a = αr.
- Solving: a = mg/(m + I/r²). The drum's inertia acts like an extra mass I/r².
- Example: I = 0.5 kg m², r = 0.2 m, m = 10 kg gives a ≈ 4.36 m/s² and T ≈ 54.5 N.

Energy and momentum for rotating bodies
- Kinetic energy of rotation about a fixed axis: ½Iω².
- General plane motion: T = ½mv_G² + ½I_Gω².
- Power transmitted by a shaft: P = Mω.
- Angular momentum about a fixed axis H = Iω; angular impulse ∫M dt = ΔH.

Exam tips: always take moments about the fixed axis (or the centre of mass), write down the kinematic constraint linking linear and angular motion, and quote the moment of inertia formula you use with its axis.

cards.f: Unit vector along a line AB
cards.b: u = (r_B − r_A)/|r_B − r_A|; a force of magnitude F along AB is F u.
A·B = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z = |A||B| cos θ; gives angles and components along lines.
A × B = (A_yB_z − A_zB_y, A_zB_x − A_xB_z, A_xB_y − A_yB_x), perpendicular to both; B × A = −A × B.

cards.f: Moment of a force about a point
cards.b: M_O = r × F, with r from O to any point on the line of action; in 2D, M_z = xF_y − yF_x.
The moment of a force equals the sum of the moments of its components about the same point.
M_u = u·(r × F), where u is a unit vector along the axis.
Two equal, opposite, parallel forces; zero resultant force, moment Fd about every point.

cards.f: Equilibrium equations for a planar rigid body
cards.b: ΣF_x = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣM = 0 about any point; at most three unknowns can be found per body.
A single force perpendicular to the supporting surface.
Two force components (horizontal and vertical); no moment.
Two force components and a moment.
The unknown reactions can all be found from equilibrium alone (three suitably arranged reactions for a planar body).
Fewer than three reactions, or three that are all parallel or concurrent, so the body cannot resist every load.
Tension along the cable, pulling away from the body; a cable cannot carry compression.
Equal to the area under the load diagram, acting through the centroid of that area.
w₀L/2 acting 2L/3 from the zero end (L/3 from the peak).
x̄ = ΣA_i x̄_i/ΣA_i; holes enter as negative areas.
One third of the height from the base (the intersection of the medians).
4r/(3π) from the diameter, on the axis of symmetry.

cards.f: Centre of gravity vs centre of mass
cards.b: They coincide in a uniform gravity field; centroid equals centre of mass for a homogeneous body of uniform thickness.
Q = ∫y dA = Aȳ; zero about an axis through the centroid.
A wall is safe against toppling about its toe if the restoring moment of its weight exceeds the overturning moment.
F ≤ μ_s N; F equals μ_s N only when slip is impending.
F = μ_k N while sliding, opposing the relative velocity; μ_k is usually below μ_s.
φ = arctan μ_s; a block on a slope steeper than φ slides under its own weight.

cards.f: Force to push a block up a slope (parallel push, impending)
cards.b: P = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ).
Compare P to slide (μW) with P to tip about the edge (Wb/2h); the smaller occurs first.
Assume no slip, solve for F, check F ≤ μ_s N; if not, it slides and F = μ_k N.
T₁/T₂ = e^(μβ), β in radians: friction grows exponentially with wrap angle.
v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, s = ½(u + v)t; only for constant a.
Equals the displacement over that interval.
Fall time √(2h/g); horizontal distance = launch speed × fall time.
a_n = v²/ρ, directed towards the centre of curvature.
a_t = dv/dt, along the path; zero at constant speed.

cards.f: Acceleration as a function of position
cards.b: Use a = v dv/ds, then integrate ∫v dv = ∫a ds.
v_B/A = v_B − v_A: the velocity of B as seen by an observer moving with A (translating frame).
ΣF = ma, applied in an inertial frame using all external forces on the body.

cards.f: Apparent weight in an accelerating lift
cards.b: N = m(g + a) when accelerating upwards; m(g − a) when accelerating downwards.

cards.f: Connected bodies over a pulley (smooth, light, inextensible)
cards.b: Same magnitude of acceleration for each body; write ΣF = ma for each and solve together.

cards.f: Maximum braking deceleration on a level road
cards.b: μg (friction limit); stopping distance v²/(2μg).
ΣF_n = mv²/ρ towards the centre of curvature; supplied by real forces only.

cards.f: Design speed of a frictionless banked curve
cards.b: v = √(rg tan θ).

cards.f: Maximum speed on a flat bend
cards.b: v = √(μgr), when friction alone provides the centripetal force.
The speed at which drag balances weight, so the net force and acceleration are zero.
T₁ + ΣU₁→₂ = T₂, where U includes the work of all forces (friction negative).
V_e = ½kx², with x the extension or compression from the natural length.
P = F·v; for a vehicle climbing at steady speed against gravity, P = mgv sin θ.
∫F dt = Δ(mv), a vector equation.
Total momentum of the colliding bodies is conserved because the impact forces are internal and brief.
e = speed of separation/speed of approach; 1 elastic, 0 perfectly plastic.

cards.f: Why energy is not conserved across a plastic impact
cards.b: Kinetic energy is lost to deformation, heat and sound; use momentum conservation for the impact itself.
V = Mv/(M + m), with v = √(2gh) just before a plastic impact.

cards.f: Moment of inertia of a thin rod
cards.b: mL²/12 about its centre; mL²/3 about one end.

cards.f: Moment of inertia of a solid disc
cards.b: mr²/2 about its central axis (thin ring: mr²).
I = I_G + md², with d the distance between the centroidal axis and the parallel axis.
ΣM_O = I_Oα about a fixed axis O.
Rope speed = ωr and acceleration = αr, where r is the drum radius.
½Iω² about a fixed axis; general plane motion: ½mv_G² + ½I_Gω².
P = Mω (torque × angular speed in rad/s).
k such that I = mk²; the distance at which the whole mass would give the same I.

questions.q: Two forces act at a point: 30 kN horizontally and 40 kN vertically. What is their resultant?
options: 50 kN at 53.1° to the 30 kN force
50 kN at 36.9° to the 30 kN force
questions.why: The forces are perpendicular, so R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 kN at arctan(40/30) = 53.1° to the 30 kN force. 70 kN adds the magnitudes as if the forces were in line. 36.9° is arctan(30/40), the angle to the 40 kN force rather than the 30 kN one. 10 kN subtracts the magnitudes, which only applies to opposing collinear forces.

questions.q: A force F = (3i + 4j) kN acts at the point (2, 1) m. What is its moment about the origin?
questions.why: M_z = xF_y − yF_x = 2 × 4 − 1 × 3 = 5 kN m; positive z means anticlockwise. Clockwise reverses the sign convention of the cross product. 11 kN m adds the two products instead of subtracting them. 11.2 kN m multiplies the magnitudes |r||F| = √5 × 5, which ignores the angle between r and F.

questions.q: A force F = (10i + 20j − 5k) N acts at the point r = (2i + k) m. (a) Find the component of F along the line through the origin in the direction (2i + 2j + k). (b) Find the angle between F and that line. (c) Find the moment of F about the origin.
A 6 m simply supported beam AB carries a uniformly distributed load of 4 kN/m over its full length and a 12 kN point load 2 m from A. What is the reaction at A?
questions.why: Moments about B: 6R_A = 12 × 4 + 24 × 3 = 120, so R_A = 20 kN. 16 kN is R_B, the other support's reaction. 18 kN splits the total 36 kN equally, ignoring the off-centre point load. 24 kN gives the whole point load to A and adds half the UDL, as if the point load sat directly over A.

questions.q: How many independent unknown reaction components does a fixed (built-in) support provide to a planar structure?
options: Three: two forces and a moment
One: a force normal to the surface
Six: three forces and three moments
questions.why: A fixed support stops translation in both directions and rotation, so it provides two forces and a moment. Two forces describes a pin, which allows rotation. A single normal force describes a roller. Six components apply to a fixed support in 3D, not a planar structure.

questions.q: A 500 N traffic signal hangs from a ring supported by two cables. Cable 1 makes 40° with the horizontal and cable 2 makes 60° with the horizontal, on opposite sides. Find the tension in each cable.
markScheme: FBD of the ring with T₁, T₂ and 500 N
questions.modelAnswer: Equilibrium of the ring. Horizontal: T₁ cos 40° = T₂ cos 60°, so T₁ = T₂ × 0.5/0.766 = 0.653T₂. Vertical: T₁ sin 40° + T₂ sin 60° = 500, so 0.653T₂ × 0.643 + 0.866T₂ = 500, i.e. 1.286T₂ = 500. Hence T₂ ≈ 389 N and T₁ ≈ 0.653 × 389 ≈ 254 N. The steeper cable carries more of the load, as expected.

questions.q: A T-section has a 120 mm × 20 mm flange on top of a 20 mm × 100 mm web (total height 120 mm). How far is the centroid above the bottom of the web?
questions.why: ȳ = (2000 × 50 + 2400 × 110)/4400 ≈ 82.7 mm. 60 mm is half the total height, which would only be right for a symmetric section. 80 mm averages the two part centroids (50 and 110) without weighting by area. 37.3 mm is the correct distance measured from the top, reported as if it were from the bottom.

questions.q: A beam carries a load that increases linearly from 0 at one end to 9 kN/m at the other over 6 m. What is the resultant?
options: 27 kN acting 4 m from the zero end
54 kN acting 3 m from the zero end
27 kN acting 3 m from the zero end
27 kN acting 2 m from the zero end
questions.why: Resultant = ½ × 9 × 6 = 27 kN through the triangle's centroid, 2L/3 = 4 m from the zero end. 54 kN at 3 m treats the load as uniform at its peak value. 27 kN at 3 m puts the correct magnitude at the midpoint, which only suits a uniform load. 2 m is L/3, the right fraction measured from the wrong (zero) end.

questions.q: A cantilever 3 m long is built in at A and free at B. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 5 kN/m over its whole length and a 10 kN point load at B. Find the reactions at A.
markScheme: FBD with vertical reaction V_A, moment M_A (and H_A = 0)
UDL resultant 15 kN at 1.5 m from A
Sense of M_A stated (resisting the clockwise moment of the loads, for a cantilever to the right)
questions.modelAnswer: The fixed support at A provides H_A, V_A and a moment M_A. There are no horizontal loads, so H_A = 0. The UDL's resultant is 5 × 3 = 15 kN acting at 1.5 m from A. Vertical equilibrium: V_A = 15 + 10 = 25 kN upwards. Moments about A: the loads produce 15 × 1.5 + 10 × 3 = 22.5 + 30 = 52.5 kN m (clockwise for a cantilever projecting to the right), so the wall must supply M_A = 52.5 kN m anticlockwise (a hogging moment).

questions.q: A 200 kg crate rests on a floor with μ_s = 0.4 and μ_k = 0.3 (g = 9.81 m/s²). A horizontal push of 700 N is applied. What happens?
options: It stays at rest and the friction force is 700 N
It slides and the friction force is 589 N
It stays at rest and the friction force is 785 N
It stays at rest and the friction force is zero, because nothing moves
questions.why: The maximum static friction is 0.4 × 1962 = 785 N. Since 700 N is less, the crate does not move and friction just balances the push: F = 700 N. 589 N is μ_k N, which applies only once sliding has started. 785 N is the limiting value, which friction reaches only at impending slip. Friction is not zero, because it is what stops the 700 N push from moving the crate.

questions.q: A uniform box 1 m wide and 2 m tall rests on a floor with μ_s = 0.5. A horizontal force P is applied 1.5 m above the floor and slowly increased. What happens first?
options: It slides, when P = W/2, because tipping needs P = 2W/3
questions.why: Tipping about the front edge needs P × 1.5 = W × 0.5, so P = W/3, smaller than the sliding force μW = W/2: it tips first. 'Slides at W/2' ignores the possibility of tipping. Tipping at 2W/3 uses the full 1 m width as the weight's moment arm instead of half the width. W/4 takes the push as acting at the top of the box (2 m) rather than at 1.5 m.

questions.q: A 50 kg block sits on a plane inclined at 20°, with μ_s = 0.25. (a) Will it stay at rest unaided? (b) Find the force parallel to the plane needed to start pushing it up the slope. (c) Find the smallest force parallel to the plane that will stop it sliding down.
markScheme: Up: P = mg(sin 20° + μ cos 20°) ≈ 283 N
Down (friction up the slope): P = mg(sin 20° − μ cos 20°) ≈ 52.5 N
Friction direction correctly reversed between (b) and (c)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Weight mg = 490.5 N. The block slips unaided if tan θ > μ_s: tan 20° = 0.364 > 0.25, so it slides down. (b) N = 490.5 cos 20° = 460.9 N. Pushing up the slope, friction acts down the slope: P = mg sin 20° + μN = 167.8 + 115.2 ≈ 283 N. (c) To hold it, friction acts up the slope (opposing the tendency to slide down): P = mg sin 20° − μN = 167.8 − 115.2 ≈ 52.5 N.

questions.q: A car starts from rest, accelerates at 2 m/s² for 10 s and then travels at constant speed for a further 5 s. How far does it travel in total?
questions.why: Phase 1: ½ × 2 × 10² = 100 m, reaching 20 m/s. Phase 2: 20 × 5 = 100 m. Total 200 m. 225 m applies s = ½at² over the full 15 s, as if it kept accelerating. 300 m multiplies the final speed by the total time, ignoring the slower start. 100 m counts only the accelerating phase.

questions.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a 20 m cliff (g = 9.81 m/s², no air resistance). How far from the foot of the cliff does it land?
questions.why: Fall time t = √(2h/g) = √(40/9.81) ≈ 2.02 s, so the distance is 15 × 2.02 ≈ 30.3 m. 61.2 m uses t = 2h/g, forgetting the square root. 22.9 m is v²/g, the level-ground range formula at 45°, which does not apply to a horizontal throw from a height. 21.4 m uses t = √(h/g), dropping the factor of 2 from h = ½gt².

questions.q: A car travels round a horizontal curve of radius 100 m, increasing its speed uniformly from 15 m/s to 25 m/s in 8 s. Find the magnitude of its acceleration at the instant its speed is 20 m/s, and explain each component.
markScheme: a_n = v²/ρ = 400/100 = 4.0 m/s² towards the centre
a_t changes speed; a_n changes direction
questions.modelAnswer: The tangential component is the rate of change of speed: a_t = (25 − 15)/8 = 1.25 m/s², along the direction of travel. The normal component comes from the change of direction: a_n = v²/ρ = 20²/100 = 4.0 m/s², towards the centre of the curve. The two are perpendicular, so |a| = √(1.25² + 4.0²) ≈ 4.19 m/s². Even if the speed were constant, the car would still accelerate at 4.0 m/s² towards the centre.

questions.q: An 80 kg person stands in a lift that is accelerating upwards at 2 m/s² (g = 9.81 m/s²). What force does the floor exert on them?
questions.why: N − mg = ma, so N = 80 × (9.81 + 2) ≈ 945 N. 785 N is the weight, which applies only at constant velocity. 625 N uses g − a, the case of downward acceleration. 160 N is ma alone, forgetting that the floor must also support the weight.

questions.q: A 10 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is connected by a light string over a smooth pulley to a hanging 5 kg mass. What is the acceleration of the system?
questions.why: The only driving force is the hanging weight 5g, which accelerates both masses: a = 5g/15 ≈ 3.27 m/s². 4.91 m/s² divides by the table block's 10 kg only, leaving out the hanging mass's own inertia. 9.81 m/s² is free fall, which ignores the string. 6.54 m/s² uses 10g/15, swapping the masses as if the table block were hanging.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car travelling at 25 m/s on a level road brakes as hard as possible without skidding. The coefficient of friction between tyres and road is 0.7. Find the deceleration, the stopping distance and the stopping time. How does the stopping distance depend on the car's mass?
markScheme: Mass cancels, so stopping distance is independent of mass (in this model)
questions.modelAnswer: The maximum friction force is F = μN = μmg = 0.7 × 1200 × 9.81 ≈ 8240 N. Newton's second law gives a = F/m = μg = 0.7 × 9.81 ≈ 6.87 m/s². Using v² = u² − 2as with v = 0: s = 25²/(2 × 6.87) ≈ 45.5 m. Time t = u/a = 25/6.87 ≈ 3.64 s. Because both the friction force and the inertia are proportional to m, the mass cancels: in this simple model the braking distance depends only on speed and μ (but it rises with the square of the speed).

questions.q: A spring of stiffness 2000 N/m is compressed 0.1 m and released, launching a 0.5 kg block along a smooth horizontal surface. What is the block's launch speed?
questions.why: ½kx² = ½mv² gives v = √(kx²/m) = √(2000 × 0.01/0.5) = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s. 4.47 m/s comes from writing ½kx² = mv², dropping the ½ from the kinetic energy only. 20 m/s uses the spring force kx in place of the energy, √(kx/m). 40 m/s is kx²/m, which forgets to take the square root.

questions.q: A 1500 kg vehicle climbs a slope (sin θ = 0.05) at a steady 20 m/s. Ignoring all resistances except gravity, what power must the engine deliver?
questions.why: P = Fv with F = mg sin θ = 1500 × 9.81 × 0.05 ≈ 736 N, so P ≈ 736 × 20 ≈ 14.7 kW. 294 kW uses the full weight mg instead of its component along the slope. 300 kW is the kinetic energy ½mv² = 300 kJ, which is an energy, not a power, and is constant at steady speed anyway. 37 W divides the force by the speed instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A 2000 kg pile-driver hammer falls freely through 1.5 m onto a 500 kg pile. The impact is perfectly plastic, and the pile and hammer then move together, driving the pile 0.1 m into the ground. Find (a) the hammer speed at impact, (b) the common speed after impact, (c) the kinetic energy lost in the impact, and (d) the average ground resistance.
markScheme: KE before 29.4 kJ, after 23.5 kJ; loss ≈ 5.9 kJ
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Energy conservation during the fall: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 1.5) ≈ 5.42 m/s. (b) Momentum is conserved in the impact: 2000 × 5.42 = 2500V, so V ≈ 4.34 m/s. (c) KE before = ½ × 2000 × 5.42² = 29 430 J; KE after = ½ × 2500 × 4.34² ≈ 23 544 J; about 5.9 kJ (20 %) is lost in the impact. (d) During penetration, the ground resistance R acts upwards and gravity on 2500 kg acts downwards over 0.1 m, removing the kinetic energy: (R − 2500 × 9.81) × 0.1 = 23 544, so R = 235 440 + 24 525 ≈ 260 kN.

questions.q: What is the moment of inertia of a uniform 3 kg rod, 2 m long, about an axis through one end perpendicular to the rod?
questions.why: I_end = mL²/3 = 3 × 4/3 = 4 kg m². 1 kg m² is mL²/12, the value about the centre, without the parallel axis term. 12 kg m² is mL², as if all the mass sat at the far end. 6 kg m² is mL²/2, the formula for a solid disc about its axis.

questions.q: A uniform rod 2 m long is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its initial angular acceleration (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
questions.why: ΣM = Iα: mg(L/2) = (mL²/3)α, so α = 3g/(2L) ≈ 7.36 rad/s². 4.91 rad/s² is g/L, which treats the rod as a point mass at its end. 14.7 rad/s² is 3g/L, taking the weight's moment arm as L instead of L/2. 9.81 rad/s² confuses the linear acceleration g with an angular acceleration.

questions.q: A 10 kg mass hangs from a light rope wound round a drum of radius 0.2 m and moment of inertia 0.5 kg m² about its fixed axle (frictionless). The system is released from rest. Find the acceleration of the mass, the rope tension and the drum's angular acceleration.
questions.modelAnswer: For the mass (down positive): 98.1 − T = 10a. For the drum: 0.2T = 0.5α. No slip: a = 0.2α, so α = 5a and T = 0.5 × 5a/0.2 = 12.5a. Substituting: 98.1 − 12.5a = 10a, so a = 98.1/22.5 ≈ 4.36 m/s². Then T = 12.5 × 4.36 ≈ 54.5 N (less than the 98.1 N weight, as it must be) and α = 4.36/0.2 ≈ 21.8 rad/s². The drum behaves like an extra mass I/r² = 12.5 kg.

questions.q:
A beam ABC is pinned at A and supported on a roller at B, 6 m from A. It overhangs to C, 8 m from A. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over AB and a 20 kN point load at C. Self-weight is neglected.
(a) Draw the free body diagram and find the reactions at A and B. [7]
(b) Check your answer using a moment equation you did not use in (a). [3]
(c) Replace the applied loads by a single equivalent resultant force and give its position from A. [4]
(d) The point load at C is increased to P. Find the value of P at which the reaction at A becomes zero, and explain what would happen if P were increased further with a roller (rather than a pin) at A. [6]
markScheme: (a) FBD: A_x, A_y at the pin; R_B vertical at the roller; 60 kN UDL resultant at 3 m; 20 kN at 8 m
(c) Resultant 80 kN down at x̄ = 340/80 = 4.25 m from A
(d) Moments about B with A_y = 0: 60 × 3 = 2P ⇒ P = 90 kN
(d) Beyond 90 kN, A would need to pull down; a roller cannot, so the beam would lift off at A and rotate about B (a mechanism)
Clear statement of sign convention and units
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The FBD shows a pin at A with components A_x and A_y, a vertical roller reaction R_B at B, the UDL over AB (resultant 10 × 6 = 60 kN acting at 3 m from A) and 20 kN down at C (8 m from A). There are no horizontal loads, so A_x = 0. Moments about A (clockwise positive): 60 × 3 + 20 × 8 − 6R_B = 0, so R_B = 340/6 ≈ 56.7 kN upwards. Vertical equilibrium: A_y + 56.7 = 60 + 20, so A_y ≈ 23.3 kN upwards.

(b) Moments about B: the UDL resultant is 3 m to the left of B and the point load 2 m to its right. 6A_y = 60 × 3 − 20 × 2 = 180 − 40 = 140, so A_y = 23.3 kN, agreeing with (a).

(c) The total load is 60 + 20 = 80 kN downwards. Its moment about A is 60 × 3 + 20 × 8 = 340 kN m, so the single resultant acts at x̄ = 340/80 = 4.25 m from A. As a further check, the reactions can be found from this single force: R_B = 80 × 4.25/6 ≈ 56.7 kN.

(d) With a load P at C, moments about B give 6A_y = 60 × 3 − 2P. A_y becomes zero when 2P = 180, i.e. P = 90 kN. For P > 90 kN, A_y would have to act downwards to hold the beam. A pin can provide that, but a roller (or a simple bearing) cannot pull down, so the beam would lift off at A and rotate about B: the support system would become a mechanism. In practice, overhanging beams and cantilevered canopies are checked for this uplift, and holding-down bolts or a counterweight are provided.

questions.q:
A road curve has a radius of 80 m and is banked at 10° to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction between tyres and road is 0.3. A car of mass 1200 kg travels round the curve at constant speed. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) Find the design speed at which no friction is needed. [5]
(b) Find the maximum speed before the car slides up the slope. [7]
(c) Show whether the car could slide down the slope when stationary. [3]
(d) The car takes the bend at 20 m/s. Find the friction coefficient required and comment. Compare with the maximum speed on an unbanked curve of the same radius. [5]
markScheme: (a) FBD: weight, normal reaction perpendicular to the road; N sin θ = mv²/r, N cos θ = mg
(b) Friction down the slope at the limit; N cos θ − F sin θ = mg; N sin θ + F cos θ = mv²/r; F = μN
(b) v² = rg(sin θ + μ cos θ)/(cos θ − μ sin θ) ⇒ v ≈ 19.9 m/s (≈ 71.5 km/h)
(c) Stationary: slides only if tan θ > μ; tan 10° = 0.176 < 0.3 so it stays put
(d) At 20 m/s: solving gives N ≈ 12.6 kN, F ≈ 3.86 kN, F/N ≈ 0.306 > 0.3 ⇒ car slides outwards (just)
(d) Unbanked: v_max = √(μgr) ≈ 15.3 m/s; banking raises the safe speed
Correct resolution of forces in horizontal (n) and vertical directions
questions.modelAnswer:
Resolve horizontally (towards the centre, the n direction) and vertically, since the car's acceleration v²/r is horizontal.

(a) With no friction: N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg), so v = √(rg tan θ) = √(80 × 9.81 × 0.1763) ≈ 11.8 m/s (about 42 km/h).

(b) Above the design speed the car tends to slide up and out, so friction F acts down the slope. Vertical: N cos θ − F sin θ = mg. Horizontal: N sin θ + F cos θ = mv²/r. At the limit F = μN. Dividing the second by the first: v²/(rg) = (sin θ + μ cos θ)/(cos θ − μ sin θ) = (0.1736 + 0.2954)/(0.9848 − 0.0521) = 0.4690/0.9327 ≈ 0.503. So v² ≈ 0.503 × 80 × 9.81 ≈ 394.7 and v ≈ 19.9 m/s (about 71.5 km/h).

(c) A stationary car slides down only if tan θ > μ_s. tan 10° = 0.176 < 0.3, so friction can hold it: there is no minimum speed for this curve.

(d) At 20 m/s, mv²/r = 1200 × 400/80 = 6000 N. Solving N cos θ − F sin θ = 11 772 and N sin θ + F cos θ = 6000 gives N ≈ 12 640 N and F ≈ 3865 N, so the required coefficient is F/N ≈ 0.306. This just exceeds 0.3, so the car would start to slide outwards; 20 m/s is just above the maximum of 19.9 m/s found in (b). On an unbanked curve friction alone provides the centripetal force, so v_max = √(μgr) = √(0.3 × 9.81 × 80) ≈ 15.3 m/s. Banking (superelevation) therefore raises the safe speed by about 30 % here, which is why highway and railway curves are banked, and why wet roads (lower μ) need lower speeds.
